source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 12 (PDF 261-279, printed 258-276); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 12 (Nuclear and Particle Physics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the structure of the atomic nucleus. Define atomic number, mass number and neutron number and give the relation between them. What are isotopes? Define the unified mass unit. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Constituents: The nucleus comprises two types of particles, protons and neutrons, together called nucleons.
Proton: the nucleus of the simplest atom, hydrogen (protium); charge +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (same magnitude as the electron's); mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
Neutron: pointed out in 1932 by James Chadwick; electrically neutral; mass nearly the same as the proton's.
A hydrogen nucleus is a single proton; all other nuclei contain both. The different nuclei are called nuclides.

Atomic number Z: the number of protons in a nucleus.
Mass number A: the total number of nucleons (neutrons + protons).
Neutron number N:
N = A − Z ... (12.1)
A nucleus is written ᴬ_Z X, where X is the chemical symbol of the element.

Isotopes: nuclei with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon always has 6 protons but may have 6, 7 or 8 neutrons: ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C, ¹⁴₆C. ¹²₆C and ¹³₆C are stable; ¹⁴₆C is unstable and decays into nitrogen with emission of β and neutrino particles.

Unified mass unit: 1 u is exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
1 u = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931 MeV
In this unit: proton 1.007276 u, neutron 1.008665 u, electron 0.00055 u.

book_ref.quote: The atomic nucleus comprises two types of particles: protons and neutrons.

blocks.prompt: 2 An iron nucleus is ⁵⁶₂₆Fe. Find (i) its number of neutrons (ii) the total mass of its protons and neutrons taken separately, in u and in kg (iii) the energy equivalent of this mass in MeV. (Proton 1.007276 u, neutron 1.008665 u, 1 u = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931 MeV) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use N = A − Z, then add Z proton masses and N neutron masses; convert with the given values of 1 u.

book_ref.quote: In this unit the mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and that of a neutron is 1.008665 u

blocks.final_answer: N = 30; mass = 56.449 u = 9.37 × 10⁻²⁶ kg; energy = 5.26 × 10⁴ MeV

blocks.prompt: 3 What are the fundamental forces of nature? Describe each of the four fundamental forces and compare their relative strength and range. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All interactions in the universe are governed by four basic forces, the fundamental forces. They control how objects move and interact from atoms to galaxies.

(i) Gravitational force: the weakest of the four but a long-range force; always attractive. The force between two bodies is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It is significant for massive objects like the sun and giant planets, but negligibly weak on an atomic level.

(ii) Electromagnetic force: responsible for electric and magnetic field interactions. Like gravity it follows an inverse square law but is much stronger. It governs atomic structure, chemical bonding, electricity, magnetism and light. Maxwell (1861) unified electricity and magnetism by four equations, showing they are two aspects of one force.

(iii) Strong nuclear force: the strongest attractive force. With only gravity and electromagnetism the nucleus would fly apart; its stability needs this force. It holds nuclei together, exists only inside the nucleus (short-range) and attracts all nucleons alike; protons attract via it while repelling electrically; neutrons attract other nucleons via it.

(iv) Weak nuclear force: responsible for radioactive decay, particularly beta decay, and interactions involving neutrinos. It can change the identity of particles, so it is essential for fusion in stars.

Comparison (Table 12.1):

book_ref.quote: all interactions in the universe are governed by the four basic forces known as fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 4 Using the relative strengths in Table 12.1, find how many times (i) the strong force is stronger than the weak force (ii) the electromagnetic force is stronger than gravity (iii) the weak force is stronger than gravity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Each ratio is one relative strength divided by the other; divide powers of ten by subtracting exponents.

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 5 What are anti-particles? Explain the process of pair production. Why is a nucleus necessary for it, and what is the minimum photon energy required? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Anti-particles: Paul Dirac predicted in 1928 that fundamental particles have anti-particles. An anti-particle has the same rest mass as its particle but opposite charge. The positron e⁺ is the anti-particle of the electron: same rest mass, positive charge of the same magnitude. It was the first anti-particle discovered (Anderson, 1932, cloud chamber). Anti-particles are written with a bar, e.g. anti-proton p̄, antineutrino ν̄. The antiproton was discovered in 1955 by Segre and Chamberlain using a particle accelerator.

Pair production: When a gamma ray photon (high-energy photon) passes near an atomic nucleus, it disappears and an electron-positron pair is emitted (Fig. 12.1):
γ → e⁻ + e⁺ (near a nucleus)

Role of the nucleus: The presence of a third particle such as a nucleus, which recoils during the collision, is necessary to conserve linear momentum and energy at the same time. So pair production cannot take place in vacuum or space.

Minimum energy: By mass-energy equivalence the minimum photon energy equals the sum of the rest mass energies of the created particles:
Emin = 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV
A photon with less than 1.02 MeV cannot produce a pair; with more than 1.02 MeV, the excess goes into the kinetic energies of the particles:
Ephoton = 1.02 MeV + K.E.(e⁻) + K.E.(e⁺)

Pair production satisfies the conservation of charge (0 = −e + e), momentum and energy.

book_ref.quote: According to the law of mass-energy equivalence, the minimum energy of a photon for pair production

blocks.prompt: 6 A gamma photon of energy 2.50 MeV produces an electron-positron pair near a nucleus. Find (i) the total kinetic energy of the pair (ii) the kinetic energy of each particle if shared equally (iii) the total kinetic energy in joules. (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Subtract the pair's rest mass energy 1.02 MeV from the photon energy; the rest is kinetic energy.

book_ref.quote: the excess energy goes into the kinetic energies of the particles

steps: Rest mass energy of the pair = 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV

blocks.prompt: 7 What is annihilation of matter? Explain the annihilation of an electron and a positron, showing how energy and momentum are conserved. Give other examples of annihilation. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Annihilation is the opposite process of pair production: a particle and its anti-particle meet and their mass changes into energy.

Electron-positron annihilation: When an electron and a positron interact, they annihilate into two gamma ray photons (Fig. 12.2):
e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ

Energy: For an electron and a positron at rest, the total rest mass energy is 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV. This appears as two photons, each of energy
E = m₀c² = 0.51 MeV
which equals the rest mass energy of an electron or a positron.

Momentum: The pair at rest has zero total momentum. The two photons share the energy equally and move in opposite directions, so their total momentum is also zero. Thus energy and momentum are conserved in the annihilation reaction. Charge is conserved too: −e + e = 0.

Other examples: annihilation of other particles with their anti-particles, e.g. proton and antiproton, lepton and antilepton, quark and antiquark.

High-energy collisions at CERN show that some mass of colliding particles changes into electromagnetic radiation according to Einstein's equation, and the left-over mass appears as new sub-atomic particles.

book_ref.quote: when an electron and a positron interact to each other they annihilate into two gamma ray photons

blocks.prompt: 8 An electron and a positron, both at rest, annihilate. Taking the electron's mass as 0.00055 u and 1 u = 931 MeV, find (i) the energy of each gamma photon (ii) the total energy released in MeV and in joules. (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Each photon carries the rest mass energy of one particle (the positron has the same mass as the electron); add both for the total.

book_ref.quote: In an annihilation reaction energy and momentum are conserved.

steps: Rest mass energy of one electron: m₀c² = 0.00055 × 931 = 0.512 MeV

blocks.prompt: 9 What is radioactivity? Distinguish natural and artificial radioactivity. Describe how α, β and γ radiations behave in an electric field and what this shows about them. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Radioactivity: Nuclei with atomic numbers greater than 82 are naturally unstable and spontaneously emit radiations. Such nuclei are radioactive, and this emission is natural radioactivity. The radiations are of three types: α-particles, β-particles and γ-radiations.

Artificial radioactivity: Unstable isotopes can be produced in the laboratory by nuclear reactions, when a stable element is bombarded with high-energy particles such as neutrons, protons, α-particles or γ-rays. Such radioactive isotopes are called radioisotopes or radionuclides.

Behaviour in an electric field (Fig. 12.4):
α-particles: deflect towards the negative terminal, so they carry positive charge. Emitted at a few percent of the speed of light, but travel only several centimetres in air due to their large mass.
β-particles: deflect towards the positive terminal, so they carry negative charge. Their deflection is greater than that of α-particles, so they are lighter. They are fast electrons with speeds up to 0.9995 of the speed of light.
γ-radiations: pass without deflection, so they have no charge. They are electromagnetic radiations (photons) moving with the speed of light, with the highest penetrating power but the lowest ionization power.

The emission of α, β and γ from the nucleus is called α-decay, β-decay and γ-decay respectively.

book_ref.quote: These radiations are of three types, α-particles, β-particles and γ-radiations.

blocks.prompt: 10 Using the typical ionization values of Table 12.2 (α about 10⁴ and β about 10² ion pairs per mm of air), find the number of ion pairs produced by (i) an α-particle travelling 3.5 cm in air (ii) a β-particle travelling 2.0 m in air. (iii) How many times more ion pairs per mm does the α-particle produce? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert each path to mm and multiply by the ion pairs per mm; the ratio of the per-mm values gives (iii).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

steps: α path: 3.5 cm = 35 mm; ion pairs = 35 × 10⁴ = 3.5 × 10⁵
β path: 2.0 m = 2000 mm; ion pairs = 2000 × 10² = 2.0 × 10⁵

blocks.prompt: 11 What is α-decay? Write its general equation and explain the changes in the parent nucleus with an example. What is meant by transmutation and by the disintegration energy (Q-value)? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cause: In a heavy nucleus the electrostatic repulsion between its many protons acts across the whole nucleus, while the strong nuclear force acts only between neighbouring nucleons. The nucleus becomes unstable and emits an α-particle.

α-particle: equivalent to a helium nucleus, two protons and two neutrons. The nucleus loses two protons and two neutrons, so Z decreases by two and A decreases by four:
ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y + ⁴₂He ... (12.2)
Here ᴬ_Z X is the parent nucleus, ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y the daughter nucleus and ⁴₂He the α-particle. Experimentally, the number of nucleons A and the electric charge are conserved.

Example: radium-226 emits an α-particle and decays into radon-222:
²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He ... (12.3)
Check: A: 226 = 222 + 4; Z: 88 = 86 + 2.

Transmutation: the daughter (Rn) is a different element from the parent (Ra). This transition of one element into another is the transmutation of elements.

Q-value: The mass of the parent nucleus is greater than the total mass of the daughter and the α-particle. So the total mass-energy (E = mc²) of the products is less than that of the original nuclide. This difference in mass-energy is the disintegration energy Q:
Q = (m_parent − m_daughter − m_α)c²

book_ref.quote: Alpha decay can be written in general as

blocks.prompt: 12 Polonium-210 (²¹⁰₈₄Po) is an α-emitter. Find (i) A and Z of the daughter nucleus (ii) the disintegration energy Q in MeV and in joules. (Masses: ²¹⁰Po = 209.982874 u, daughter = 205.974465 u, ⁴He = 4.002603 u; 1 u = 931 MeV; 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: In α-decay A falls by 4 and Z by 2; Q is the mass lost (parent minus products) times 931 MeV/u.

book_ref.quote: Thus the total mass-energy (E = mc²) of the decay products is less than the mass-energy of the original nuclide.

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain β⁻-decay and β⁺-decay. Write the decay of the nucleon and the general equation in each case, with an example. Why was the neutrino proposed? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) β⁻-decay: Nuclides with a neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) too large undergo β⁻-decay. β-particles are not orbital electrons; they are created within the nucleus at the moment of emission. A neutron decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino:
¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
The electron is emitted to conserve charge. No nucleon is lost, so A stays the same while the atomic number Z increases by one:
ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z+1) Y + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
Example: thorium-234 decays into protactinium: ²³⁴₉₀Th → ²³⁴₉₁Pa + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄

(ii) β⁺-decay: Nuclides with N/P too small for stability emit a positron (same mass as the electron, positive charge; the electron's anti-particle). A proton decays into a neutron, a positron and a neutrino; Z decreases by one, A unchanged:
ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z−1) Y + ⁰₊₁e + ν
Example: ¹⁹₁₀Ne → ¹⁹₉F + ⁰₊₁e + ν

Neutrino: proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930 so that energy is conserved in β⁻ and β⁺ decays. The neutrino and antineutrino have zero charge and very small mass, so they are very hard to observe; the neutrino was detected in 1953 by F. Reines and C. L. Cowan in a high-power nuclear reactor.

book_ref.quote: There are two types of β-decay, beta-minus decay and beta-plus decay.

blocks.prompt: 14 A free neutron decays as n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. Using the masses given in the chapter (neutron 1.008665 u, proton 1.007276 u, electron 0.00055 u) and 1 u = 931 MeV, find the energy released. Treat the antineutrino's mass as negligible. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The energy released is the mass lost (neutron minus proton and electron) times 931 MeV/u.

book_ref.quote: In this process, a neutron in the nucleus decays into a proton and an electron

blocks.final_answer: Energy released = 0.781 MeV (shared by the electron and the antineutrino)

blocks.prompt: 15 Compare the energy spectra of α-particles and β-particles emitted by a radionuclide. Explain γ-emission and summarise the properties of α, β and γ radiations. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In both α-decay and β-decay of a particular radionuclide, the same amount of energy is released each time.

α-spectrum: every emitted α-particle has the same sharply defined kinetic energy. The graph of the number of α-particles against kinetic energy shows distinct spikes (Fig. 12.5): α-particles have discrete energies.

β-spectrum: the energy is shared between the β-particle and the antineutrino (or neutrino) in varying proportions, though their sum is always the same. So the energy of an electron or positron may range from zero to a maximum value. The graph is a smooth curve (Fig. 12.6): β-particles have a continuous range of energies.
Conservation of momentum and energy applies in both α and β emission.

γ-emission: An excited nucleus goes to its ground state by emitting γ-radiation:
ᴬ_Z X* → ᴬ_Z X + γ
A and Z do not change.

Summary (Table 12.2):

book_ref.quote: In both α-decay and β-decay, for a particular radionuclide, the same amount of energy is released.

rows: Electrons or positrons from the nucleus, charge ±e
E.M. waves from excited nuclei, no charge
Ion pairs per mm in air

blocks.prompt: 16 In a certain β⁻-decay, 1.71 MeV is shared between the electron and the antineutrino. Find (i) the electron's energy when the antineutrino carries 0.96 MeV (ii) the antineutrino's energy when the electron carries 0.40 MeV (iii) the maximum possible energy of the electron. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The sum of the two energies is always 1.71 MeV; the electron has the maximum when the antineutrino gets almost nothing.

book_ref.quote: Thus in β-decay, the energy of an electron or a positron may range from zero to a maximum value.

blocks.prompt: 17 What is a fundamental particle? Explain the classification of particles into fermions and bosons, and into hadrons (baryons and mesons) and leptons, with examples. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Fundamental particle: a particle with no internal structure, i.e. indivisible. Presently quarks (which make up protons, neutrons and mesons) and leptons (electrons, positrons, neutrinos) are the basic building blocks of matter. β-decay, in which a neutron and a proton change into each other, is evidence that protons and neutrons are not fundamental.

By spin: All particles spin on their axes. Electrons, protons and neutrons have spin 1/2, the photon 1 and pions 0.
Fermions: half-spin particles; they obey Pauli's exclusion principle (only one particle of a kind in a given quantum state).
Bosons: zero or whole-number spin; they do not obey this principle and obey Bose-Einstein statistics.

By the strong force:
Hadrons: particles that experience the strong force; composite particles, e.g. protons, neutrons, pions. They are of two kinds:
  Baryons: fermions made of an odd number of quarks (usually three), e.g. proton, neutron, Λ⁰.
  Mesons: bosons made of an even number of quarks (usually a quark and an antiquark), e.g. pion, kaon.
Leptons: particles that do not experience the strong force; they interact only through weak or electromagnetic interactions. No internal structure has been found; all have spin ½ (fermions). The six leptons form three pairs: (e⁻, νₑ), (μ⁻, ν_μ), (τ⁻, ν_τ), each with its anti-particle. The best-known lepton is the electron; neutrinos rarely interact and are rarely observed.

book_ref.quote: Particles can be broadly classified based on whether they interact via the strong force.

blocks.prompt: 18 Using Table 12.3 (electron 0.511, muon 105.7, tau 1777 MeV/c²) and 1 u = 931 MeV, find (i) the muon's mass in u (ii) how many times heavier the muon is than the electron (iii) how many times heavier the tau is than the muon. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide MeV/c² by 931 to get u; ratios of masses need no conversion.

book_ref.quote: Table 12.3: The lepton family

blocks.prompt: 19 What are quarks? Name the six quark flavours with their charges. Describe the proton, the neutron and the π⁺ meson in terms of quarks, explain β⁻-decay at the quark level, and explain colour charge. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Quarks: In 1964 M. Gell-Mann and George Zweig proposed that hadrons, even protons and neutrons, are made of more fundamental entities called quarks. Quarks are truly fundamental, like leptons. They have spin and a fractional charge, and never appear on their own.

Flavours (Table 12.4): up u (+2/3), down d (−1/3), strange s (−1/3) were proposed first; charm c (+2/3), bottom b (−1/3), top t (+2/3) came later. Each antiquark has the opposite charge (ū −2/3, d̄ +1/3, ...).

Baryons have three quarks:
Proton (uud): q = 2/3 + 2/3 + (−1/3) = +1
Neutron (udd): q = 2/3 + (−1/3) + (−1/3) = 0
Mesons are quark-antiquark pairs:
π⁺ (ud̄): q = 2/3 + 1/3 = +1

β⁻-decay in quarks: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. A neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud) when a down quark changes into an up quark:
d → u + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄

Colour: Quarks have another property, colour charge (analogous to electric charge). Each flavour has one of three colours: red, green, blue; antiquarks have antired, antigreen, antiblue. A baryon has one quark of each colour and a meson a colour with its anticolour, so both are colourless (white). The strong force between colour charges is the colour force; its theory is quantum chromodynamics (QCD). The strong force between hadrons is the force between their quarks.

book_ref.quote: All hadrons are considered to be made up of combinations of quarks

blocks.prompt: 20 Using the quark charges of Table 12.4, find the charge of each combination and say whether it is a baryon or a meson: (i) uss (ii) dū (iii) cd̄ (iv) ddd. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the charges of the quarks (antiquarks have opposite charge); three quarks make a baryon, a quark-antiquark pair a meson.

book_ref.quote: Mesons are quark–antiquark pairs.

blocks.prompt: 21 How do fundamental particles interact by exchanging bosons? Name the carriers of the fundamental forces. Describe the Higgs boson and its role in giving mass to particles. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Fundamental particles: the six quarks, the six leptons and the bosons that carry the fundamental forces.

Exchange of bosons: Leptons and quarks interact by sending and receiving bosons, which 'carry' the force:
Electromagnetic force: two charged particles exchange photons.
Strong force: two quarks in a nucleus attract by exchanging gluons.
Weak nuclear force: carried by the W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons.
Gravitational force: carried by gravitons.

Higgs boson: a special particle discovered in 2012 at the large hadron collider at CERN. It is associated with the Higgs field, which permeates all of space. It is a separate fundamental boson linked to mass, not a carrier of a force.

Role in mass: Particles get mass by interacting with the Higgs field. Those that interact strongly get more mass, e.g. the carriers of the electroweak interaction W⁺, W⁻ and Z; photons do not interact with it, so their rest mass is zero.

Key facts: mass around 125 GeV; decays rapidly into other particles; gets its own mass from its interaction with the Higgs field; may be a unique portal to the conditions of the universe shortly after the Big Bang and to signs of dark matter.

book_ref.quote: Leptons and quarks interact with each other by sending and receiving bosons.

blocks.prompt: 22 The Higgs boson has a mass of about 125 GeV. Express it (i) in u (ii) in kg, and (iii) compare it with the proton's mass of 1.007276 u. (1 u = 931 MeV = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert GeV to MeV, divide by 931 for u, multiply by 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ for kg, then divide by the proton's mass.

book_ref.quote: Higgs boson has a mass of around 125 giga-electron-volts (GeV)

blocks.final_answer: (i) 134 u (ii) 2.23 × 10⁻²⁵ kg (iii) about 133 times the proton's mass

blocks.prompt: 23 State the conservation laws obeyed by all nuclear reactions and decays. Show with examples of α-decay, β⁻-decay and pair production that charge and nucleon number are conserved, and classify hadrons and non-hadrons. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All nuclear processes, such as nuclear reactions and nuclear decays, obey conservation laws:
(i) conservation of energy, momentum and charge, including the nucleon number A and the charge number Z;
(ii) conservation of baryon number;
(iii) conservation of lepton number.

α-decay: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He
A: 226 = 222 + 4; Z: 88 = 86 + 2. Both conserved; the mass-energy difference appears as the Q-value, so energy is conserved.

β⁻-decay: ¹₀n → ¹₁p + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄
A: 1 = 1 + 0; charge: 0 = +1 + (−1) + 0. The electron is emitted to conserve charge, and the antineutrino carries part of the energy so that energy is conserved.

Pair production: γ → e⁻ + e⁺ (near a nucleus)
Charge: 0 = −1 + 1. The recoiling nucleus allows momentum and energy to be conserved together.

Classification (chapter box):
Hadrons: mesons (e.g. pions, kaons) and baryons (e.g. protons, neutrons, omega, sigma and lambda particles).
Non-hadrons: leptons (electrons, muons, neutrinos), photons and gravitons.

book_ref.quote: All nuclear process such as nuclear reactions and nuclear decays obey conservation laws such as:

blocks.prompt: 24 Thorium-232 (²³²₉₀Th) decays through a series of α and β⁻ emissions into lead-208 (²⁰⁸₈₂Pb). Using conservation of nucleon number and charge number, find the number of α-particles and of β⁻-particles emitted. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Only α-decay changes A (by 4 each); count α from the change in A, then use Z to find how many β⁻ (each raises Z by 1) are needed.

book_ref.quote: conservation of energy, momentum and charge.

steps: Change in A = 232 − 208 = 24; each α removes 4 nucleons, β⁻ removes none
Each β⁻ raises Z by 1: number of β⁻ = 82 − 78 = 4

blocks.prompt: 25 Explain the asymmetry of matter and antimatter in the universe and the suggested reason for it. What are dark matter and dark energy, and why is most of the matter in the observable universe said to be plasma? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Asymmetry: Many observations show an asymmetry between matter and antimatter, one of the most remarkable features of our universe. The universe consists almost entirely of matter rather than antimatter: its ordinary matter (electrons, protons and neutrons) is mostly hydrogen and helium atoms, with no contribution of antihydrogen or anti-helium atoms.

Suggested reason: Experimental results link the asymmetry to violation of the conservation of baryon number, i.e. an imbalance between the numbers of baryons and anti-baryons. If particle-antiparticle symmetry is also violated, there would be a mechanism for making more quarks than antiquarks, more leptons than antileptons, and eventually more matter than antimatter. The problem is still a mystery.

Dark matter and dark energy: We know about only about 5% of the universe. About 27% is unknown matter called dark matter and about 68% a mysterious antigravity material called dark energy; 27% + 68% = 95% is unknown to us.

Plasma: Of the known matter, hydrogen and helium make up almost all of it, and these are almost entirely in the plasma state. Hence most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma.

book_ref.quote: Many observations show that there is the asymmetry between matter and antimatter.

blocks.prompt: 26 If 1.0 g of matter met 1.0 g of antimatter and both were completely annihilated, how much energy would be released? Use E = mc² with c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: In annihilation the whole mass of both (matter and antimatter) changes into energy; convert grams to kg first.

book_ref.quote: there are no any contribution of antihydrogen or anti-helium atoms

steps: Total mass annihilated: m = 1.0 g + 1.0 g = 2.0 g = 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg

blocks.prompt: 27 Describe the quantum field theory and the string theory of the forces between particles. What is the standard model? Describe its three categories of particles and its limitations. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Two theories explain the interactions between particles through different mediators.

(i) Quantum field theory: Each particle is represented by a quantum field, which transmits a force from one particle to another by a mediator. E.g. a positive charge produces an electric field and through it attracts a nearby negative charge. The field carries energy and momentum, which are quantized. The quanta exchanged are field particles, all bosons:
electromagnetic force: photons; strong nuclear force: gluons; weak force: W and Z bosons; gravitational force: gravitons.

(ii) String theory: Fundamental particles are not point-like but tiny vibrating strings, open or closed loops. Their vibrations determine the particle's properties, including mass and force. It is a possible theory of everything but remains unproved experimentally.

Standard model: the collection of theories that describe the smallest experimentally observed particles of matter and the interaction between energy and matter. Three categories of particles (Fig. 12.8):
Quarks and leptons: make up matter (only 5% of the universe).
Fundamental bosons: provide three forces, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force and the weak nuclear force.
Higgs boson (discovered 2012): explains how the other particles get mass.

Limitations: The model is still incomplete. It cannot explain (i) gravity (ii) dark matter (27% of the universe) (iii) dark energy (68% of the universe).

book_ref.quote: The standard model is the collection of theories that describe the smallest experimentally observed particles

blocks.prompt: 28 Using Table 12.4 (up quark 5 MeV/c², top quark 175000 MeV/c²) and 1 u = 931 MeV = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, find (i) the top quark's mass in u (ii) its mass in kg (iii) how many times heavier it is than the up quark. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide by 931 for u, multiply by 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ for kg; the ratio needs no conversion.

book_ref.quote: Matter, which makes up only 5% of the universe is composed of quarks and leptons.
